rv.q: This is, unmistakably and viscerally, real life in all its resolutely un-Hollywood imperfection.

When her husband Gary (Daniel Ryan) joins her in the kitchen, he finds more than a hot drink brewing. “I’m not sure I love you any more,” she says. Very little happens in terms of incident: this is a drama in which the action is all on an emotional level and, as such, it is excruciatingly honest and beautifully controlled by Eldridge.
What ensues in the following hour and 40 minutes is always gripping, often painfully funny, and mostly deeply sad.
The pleasure here is in two superbly convincing performances from Claire Rushbrook and Daniel Ryan, and in the rueful writing of David Eldridge, shafts of humour consistently lightening the darkness.
Rushbrook and Ryan give wonderfully nuanced performances, as they slowly peel back the layers to reveal deep-rooted pain and resentment.

It feels like a true and tender representation of a marriage in its middle stages, a drama that is tepid at times, a little plodding and soft around the edges but forging on – much like middle age itself.

But with these prosperous, well-adjusted characters grappling with nothing more significant than a dawning sense that they’ve lost control over the trajectory of their lives, the ferociously low stakes rob the piece of any dramatic energy generated by the committed performances it showcases.
Sad to say, Middle isn’t anywhere near as persuasive, lapsing into dull, meandering exchanges which, on press night anyway, prompted ripples of laughter.

It is a play that is painful and moving. The characters’ personal foibles sometimes add a leavening of humour, but it was probably the tension between them or perhaps self recognition that prompted the nervous cackles of laughter that came from some parts of the audience.
The play is much funnier than it deserves to be, given the subject matter, and at times it is heart-stoppingly sad and it asks important questions.

Polly Findlay's direction, which keeps things taut and watchful, and the fine performances hold the attention as Rick Fisher's nuanced lighting charts the progress from night to day, and the play ends, like its predecessor, with a gleam of possibility.
But, though sincere, Eldridge’s portrait feels too conservative and inconsequential.
This makes the 100-minute play too funny to be tragic, too erratic to be compelling and too uncertain to be truly raw.
It well conveys how starting up a meaningful conversation for the first time in years is like cranking up a long-seized engine.
Polly Findlay’s direction is deft and swift, and purely as individuals both characters, as played here, are heartbreakingly real.

cn.t: Eldridge's follow-up to his 2017 hit Beginning earns mostly positive reviews for its naturalistic depiction of a marriage in crisis, with critics praising the performances while finding it slower and less compelling than its predecessor.
